newsitem.title: UK: Britain sets up "Mummy Tissue Bank".
newsitem.headline: Britain sets up "Mummy Tissue Bank".

text.p: Britain is setting up the world's first Mummy Tissue Bank in an international effort to trace the diseases, sex habits and lifestyles of the ancient Egyptians.
The tissue bank -- due to open in the New Year in the northern English city of Manchester -- will be run in collaboration with U.S. and Egyptian scientists.

"There is huge opportunity to track all sorts of developments as we have preserved bodies from 5,000 years ago and people of today who are genetically the same," Rosalie David, director of the project, told Reuters.

The team will gather samples of blood, tissue and internal organs from mummies housed in museums around the world to pursue their research. Tissues from the pharaohs will be stored in Cairo as the export of royal remains from Egypt is banned.
David said her mummies -- be it ordinary Egyptians or nobility -- would initially be used to trace the development of diseases such as bilharzia, a waterborne disease prevalent in the tropics.
The tissue bank, run with the U.S. Medical Service Corporation International in Arlington, Virginia, could also be used to track family relations and migration patterns, she said.

David said colleagues in Egypt were pursuing their own research that could reveal who fathered Tutankhamun and how much the rulers of ancient Egypt engaged in incest and how much they bred with the population at large.
Tutankhamun's father is thought to be the heretic Akhenaten. His mummy is missing but Akhenaten was believed to suffer from an inherited disorder called Frohlich's disease.
If Tutankhamun also carries the Frohlich's disease gene, it will be likely that Akhenaten was his father.
